title: India Set to Make Insulting Vande Mataram a Criminal Offence as Bill Heads to Parliament
excerpt: The Prevention of Insults to National Honour Amendment Bill would extend the same statutory protections currently afforded to the national anthem to India's national song.
body:
Key Takeaways
  • The Prevention of Insults to National Honour Bill aims to criminalize insults to Vande Mataram.
  • Penalties include up to three years' imprisonment or fines for willful insults to the national song.
  • The bill follows a Supreme Court ruling that current guidelines on Vande Mataram are advisory only.
  • The Union Cabinet approved the amendment after celebrations for the song's 150th anniversary.

Based on the Prevention of Insults to National Honour Amendment Bill, 2026
  • The Indian government has listed the Prevention of Insults to National Honour (Amendment) Bill, 2026, for introduction and passage during the Monsoon Session of Parliament
  • The bill would extend criminal penalties — up to three years' imprisonment, a fine, or both — to anyone who wilfully insults the national song or disrupts its singing
  • The Union Cabinet approved the amendment in May 2026 following year-long celebrations marking 150 years of Vande Mataram
  • The Supreme Court ruled in March that existing MHA guidelines on the national song are advisory and carry no penal consequences — this bill would change that

What the Bill Proposes

India's government is poised to give the national song Vande Mataram the same legal shield that has protected the national anthem Jana Gana Mana for over five decades. According to a Lok Sabha Secretariat bulletin, the Prevention of Insults to National Honour (Amendment) Bill, 2026, has been listed for introduction, consideration and passage during the ongoing Monsoon Session of Parliament.

The bill seeks to amend the Prevention of Insults to National Honour Act, 1971, which currently penalizes insults to the national flag, the Constitution and the national anthem with imprisonment of up to three years, a fine, or both. Under the proposed amendment, wilful insult to Vande Mataram or deliberate disruption of its singing would attract identical penalties.

https://x.com/Chanakyanexus/status/2078363726156345540

Union Home Minister Amit Shah is expected to table the legislation. The Union Cabinet, chaired by Prime Minister Narendra Modi, approved the proposal in May after the conclusion of nationwide celebrations marking 150 years of the song, written by Bankim Chandra Chattopadhyay in 1875 and first published in his Bengali novel Anandamath in 1882.

> **"In December 2025, Parliament held 10-hour special discussions across both Houses on the song's 150-year legacy."**

"Delighted to share that the Union Cabinet has approved the amendment to the Prevention of Insults to National Honour Act, 1971, granting our National Song Vande Mataram the same statutory protection as the National Anthem."

— Anurag Thakur, BJP MP and former Union Minister

From Advisory to Criminal Law

The bill comes three months after the Supreme Court weighed in on the government's approach to the national song. In March, a three-judge bench led by Chief Justice Surya Kant dismissed a petition challenging a Ministry of Home Affairs circular mandating that all six stanzas of Vande Mataram be sung at official events. The court ruled that the MHA guidelines were purely advisory, used the word "may," and carried no penal consequences for non-compliance.

"We will hear all this when there are penal consequences or when it is made mandatory," the bench had observed. The new bill would do precisely that — convert what was an advisory framework into enforceable criminal law.

The January 28 MHA circular had also directed that when both the national song and the national anthem are performed at the same event, all six stanzas of Vande Mataram must be presented first. Previously, only the first two stanzas were used at official events, with the remaining portions — which invoke Hindu goddesses Durga, Lakshmi and Saraswati — typically omitted.

Political Context of the Bill
›10-hour discussions in Parliament on Vande Mataram's legacy.

Political Battle Lines

The legislation carries significant political weight. In December 2025, Parliament held 10-hour special discussions across both Houses on the song's 150-year legacy. Modi used the debate to accuse former Prime Minister Jawaharlal Nehru of diluting the song's significance for appeasement politics, referencing the 1937 Congress Working Committee decision to adopt only the first two stanzas as the official version.

The Congress has countered by highlighting its freedom fighters who were arrested while chanting Vande Mataram during the independence movement. AIMIM chief Asaduddin Owaisi has called the legislation a form of "religious imposition," arguing that the later stanzas invoke Hindu deities and are incompatible with the secular character of the Constitution.

The government has maintained that the bill is intended to formalize the song's status and does not mandate compulsory singing — only penalizes deliberate insult or disruption.

Broader Legislative Agenda

The Vande Mataram bill is part of a packed Monsoon Session agenda. Other legislation slated for consideration includes the Viksit Bharat Shiksha Adhishthan Bill, 2025, which would replace the UGC, AICTE and NCTE with a unified higher education regulator, and the Registration of Births and Deaths (Amendment) Bill, 2026, which proposes stricter rules for delayed registrations.

Broader Legislative Agenda
›Viksit Bharat Shiksha Adhishthan Bill to unify higher education regulation.
›Registration of Births and Deaths (Amendment) Bill proposed.
›Income-Tax amendment and updated MSME legislation planned.

The government also plans to introduce an Income-Tax amendment bill and updated MSME legislation during the session.

What It Means for the Diaspora

For Indians abroad, Vande Mataram holds a particular emotional resonance. The song is frequently performed at diaspora cultural events, Independence Day celebrations and community gatherings worldwide. While the bill's criminal provisions would apply only within Indian jurisdiction, the elevated legal status of the national song underscores its significance in India's national identity — a matter of cultural pride for millions of NRIs who grew up singing it in school assemblies.
